mainTopic: A husband's silence about his wife's נדר: even silence meant to annoy her ratifies it (רבי חנינא is refuted); the start of a new פרק on which vows can be cancelled
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא about how a husband ratifies (הקם) or cancels (הפר) his wife's נדר. Silence and a silent decision in the heart can ratify, but they cannot cancel. The גמרא first tries to prove from this ברייתא that even silence meant to annoy the wife ratifies. It deflects that proof by explaining that the ברייתא means plain silence (שותק סתם). Next it asks where הפר is stronger than הקם. רבי יוחנן answers that a חכם can undo a הקם but not a הפר. Then רב כהנא, רבא and רב אשי each bring a source showing that silence ratifies even when it was not meant to ratify. Each challenge ends in תיובתא, so רבי חנינא's view that a husband silent to annoy can still cancel later is refuted. The פרק נערה המאורסה then closes. A new פרק opens with a משנה listing the vows a husband can cancel, starting with vows of עינוי נפש such as bathing and adorning oneself.

steps.title: The ברייתא: silence can ratify but cannot cancel
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues listing how הקם and הפר work. Silence ratifies but does not cancel, a decision in the heart ratifies but does not cancel, and once one choice is made the other is no longer possible.
steps.simpleTranslation: Silence ratifies a vow, but silence does not cancel a vow. If he ratified it in his heart, it is ratified. If he cancelled it in his heart, it is not cancelled. Once he ratified, he cannot cancel. Once he cancelled, he cannot ratify.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its quote of a ברייתא about how a husband ratifies or cancels his wife's נדר. It is laying out the text it will use for a challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: הקם is easier to bring about than הפר. Silence alone, or a silent decision in the heart, is enough to ratify. Cancelling needs more than that. Also, each decision is final: after one is made, the husband cannot switch to the other.

keyTerms.meaning: silence: the husband says nothing about the vow
in his heart: decided silently, without speaking
he cancelled (the husband's power to annul his wife's vow)

phrases.english: that silence ratifies,
but silence does not cancel.
If he ratified in his heart, it is ratified,
if he cancelled in his heart, it is not cancelled.
If he ratified, he cannot cancel,
if he cancelled, he cannot ratify.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted at the end of the previous section of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Silence and a silent decision in the heart can ratify a נדר but cannot cancel it. After either הקם or הפר, the husband cannot switch to the other.

steps.title: Does silence meant to annoy also ratify?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that 'silence ratifies' includes even a husband who stays silent to annoy his wife. That would challenge the view that such a husband can still cancel later.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא teaches: silence ratifies. Doesn't that mean even someone who is silent in order to annoy her?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points to the words 'silence ratifies' and suggests they cover every kind of silence, even silence meant to annoy the wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even silence meant to annoy counts as ratifying, then the husband loses his chance to cancel the נדר. That goes against the opinion (רבי חנינא's) that a husband who is שותק על מנת למיקט can still cancel later.

keyTerms.meaning: is it not? (a suggested reading used as a challenge)
in order to annoy or pain her

phrases.english: It teaches: that silence ratifies,

phrases.aramaic: מַאי לָאו בְּשׁוֹתֵק עַל מְנָת לְמֵיקַט?
phrases.english: is it not referring to one who is silent in order to annoy?
phrases.notes: He means a husband who keeps quiet on purpose so his wife suffers under the vow for a while, not because he wants it to stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ברייתא just quoted to build a challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that a husband who is שותק על מנת למיקט can still cancel the נדר later.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא says silence ratifies with no limits, so it seems to include silence meant to annoy.

steps.title: No, it means silence in order to ratify
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about a husband who stays silent because he wants the נדר to stand.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It is talking about one who is silent in order to ratify.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back and limits 'silence ratifies' to a husband whose silence is meant to keep the vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ברייתא only means silence with a ratifying goal, it says nothing about silence meant to annoy. So the challenge goes away.

keyTerms.meaning: to ratify: to let the vow stand

phrases.english: No, it refers to one who is silent in order to ratify.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the ברייתא refers only to silence meant to ratify.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Silence ratifies' covers every kind of silence.
steps.terutzMaskana: It covers only silence whose purpose is to ratify.

steps.title: That would repeat 'ratified in his heart'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects that answer. Silence with the goal of ratifying is the same as 'ratifying in his heart,' which the ברייתא lists separately.
steps.simpleTranslation: But that is the same as 'if he ratified in his heart, it is ratified'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the last answer does not work, because it would make the ברייתא say the same thing twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A silent husband who means to ratify has decided in his heart to ratify. The ברייתא already has a separate line for that case. So 'silence ratifies' must be teaching something different.

keyTerms.meaning: that is the same as: points out repetition

phrases.english: That is the same as: if he ratified in his heart, it is ratified!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in step 3.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא means silence in order to ratify.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That reading makes two lines of the ברייתא say the same thing, and a ברייתא does not repeat itself for no reason.

steps.title: It means plain silence with no stated purpose
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא concludes that 'silence ratifies' means a husband who is silent with no particular intention. Silence meant to annoy is still not included.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it refers to one who is silent without any particular intention.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final reading: the ברייתא is talking about plain, unexplained silence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Plain silence is a new case, different from deciding in the heart, so the ברייתא is not repeating itself. Silence meant to annoy is still left out, so the view that such a husband can still cancel stays standing.

keyTerms.meaning: silent plainly, without any particular intention

steps.whatToRemember: 'Silence ratifies' in the ברייתא means plain silence (שותק סתם), not silence meant to annoy. So the ברייתא does not disprove that a שותק על מנת למיקט can still cancel.

phrases.english: Rather, it refers to one who is silent without specifying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected answer of step 3 after the challenge in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A new case definition: plain silence.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It means silence in order to ratify.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means silence with no particular intention, which is a separate case from ratifying in the heart.

steps.title: Where is cancelling stronger than ratifying?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא showed ways הקם is stronger than הפר. The גמרא asks where we find the opposite.
steps.simpleTranslation: We have found a stringency in ratifying over cancelling. Where do we find a stringency in cancelling over ratifying?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new question about the ברייתא. It is asking for a case where הפר is stronger than הקם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All the points so far showed that הקם happens more easily, for example through silence or a decision in the heart. The גמרא now wants an example of the reverse, so that there are stringencies in both directions.

phrases.english: We have found a stringency in ratifying over cancelling,
in cancelling over ratifying, from where do we know?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַשְׁכְּחַן חוֹמֶר בְּהָקֵם מִבְּהָפֵר, בְּהָפֵר מִבְּהָקֵם מְנָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the silence discussion to a new question about the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A case in which הפר is stronger than הקם.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: a הקם can be undone by a חכם, a הפר cannot
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that a husband may ask a חכם to undo his ratification, but he cannot ask to undo his cancellation.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: One may ask a sage to undo a ratification, but one may not ask to undo a cancellation.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives the missing example: a הפר is final in a way that a הקם is not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A husband who regrets ratifying can go to a חכם to have his הקם undone, and then he can cancel the vow. A הפר cannot be undone that way. In this one way, הפר is the stronger act.

keyTerms.meaning: one may ask a sage to undo it

steps.whatToRemember: הקם is easier to bring about (even through silence), but הפר is more final: a חכם can undo a הקם, not a הפר.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
One may request release from the ratification,
but one may not request release from the cancellation.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: נִשְׁאָלִין עַל הֶהָקֵם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A חכם can undo a הקם but not a הפר, so הפר is stronger in that it is final.

steps.title: רב כהנא challenges from a ברייתא on the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא brings a ברייתא that reads the פסוק 'if her husband stays silent' as talking about silence meant to annoy. That seems to say such silence ratifies.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא raised an objection: 'But if her husband stays silent to her...' The verse is speaking of one who is silent in order to annoy.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא opens a new challenge. He quotes a ברייתא that says the פסוק about the husband's silence is talking about silence meant to annoy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says this silence ratifies all her vows. If it is talking about a שותק על מנת למיקט, then silence meant to annoy does ratify. That goes against רבי חנינא, who said such a husband can still cancel later.

phrases.english: Rav Kahana raised an objection:
"But if her husband stays silent to her, etc."
phrases.notes: במדבר 30:15. The rest of the פסוק says he thereby ratifies all her vows.

phrases.aramaic: בְּשׁוֹתֵק עַל מְנָת לְמֵיקַט הַכָּתוּב מְדַבַּר.
phrases.english: The verse is speaking of one who is silent in order to annoy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the topic of silence meant to annoy, now challenging from a ברייתא on the פסוק.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חנינא's view that a שותק על מנת למיקט can still cancel later.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא reads the פסוק, which says silence ratifies, as talking about silence meant to annoy.

steps.title: The ברייתא asks: annoy or ratify?
steps.stepSummary: Inside the ברייתא, a question is raised: is the פסוק really about silence meant to annoy, or only about silence meant to ratify?
steps.simpleTranslation: Do you say it refers to one who is silent in order to annoy, or perhaps only to one who is silent in order to ratify?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא questions its own reading. It is setting up a proof, which comes next, that the פסוק means silence meant to annoy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא raises the other possibility: maybe the פסוק only means silence with the goal of ratifying. Asking the question this way shows that the ברייתא is about to give a reason for choosing 'to annoy.'

keyTerms.meaning: do you say?: a ברייתא formula that tests a reading
or perhaps it is only: raises the other possibility

phrases.aramaic: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בְּשׁוֹתֵק עַל מְנָת לְמֵיקַט,
phrases.english: Do you say it refers to one who is silent in order to annoy,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּשׁוֹתֵק עַל מְנָת לְקַיֵּים?
phrases.english: or is it only referring to one who is silent in order to ratify?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַתָּה אוֹמֵר בְּשׁוֹתֵק עַל מְנָת לְמֵיקַט, אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא quoted by רב כהנא, testing its own reading.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the פסוק refers to silence meant to annoy or only to silence meant to ratify.

steps.title: The ברייתא answers: one phrase is about silence to confirm, the other is about silence to annoy
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא answers its own question. The words 'כי החריש לה' already cover silence meant to confirm, so the doubled phrase 'החרש יחריש' must be about silence meant to annoy.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the פסוק already says 'because he held his peace at her,' that part is about a husband who stays silent in order to confirm. So how do I explain 'if her husband altogether holds his peace at her'? It must be about a husband who stays silent in order to annoy her.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the question from step 9. It shows that the פסוק must include silence meant to annoy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same פסוק talks about silence twice. One mention is already used up for silence meant to confirm. That leaves the doubled phrase 'החרש יחריש' free to teach something new: even silence meant to annoy confirms the נדר.

keyTerms.meaning: staying silent in order to confirm the נדר
staying silent in order to annoy (tease) the wife
so how do I explain (this other phrase)?

phrases.english: When it says "because he held his peace at her,"
then it is about one who is silent in order to confirm
that the verse is speaking.
So how do I explain
"if her husband altogether holds his peace at her"?
phrases.notes: This is the earlier part of the same פסוק, במדבר 30:15.

phrases.english: It is about one who is silent in order to annoy
that the verse is speaking!

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּשֶׁהוּא אוֹמֵר ״כִּי הֶחֱרִשׁ לָהּ״, הֲרֵי בְּשׁוֹתֵק עַל מְנָת לְקַיֵּים הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised inside the ברייתא in step 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the doubled silence phrase about silence to annoy, or only silence to confirm?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Silence to confirm is already covered by 'כי החריש לה', so 'החרש יחריש' must be about silence to annoy.

steps.title: The ברייתא refutes the earlier view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא declares that the ברייתא is a full refutation of the view that silence meant to annoy does not confirm the נדר.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rules that רב כהנא's ברייתא has knocked down the earlier view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי חנינא held that a husband who stays silent to annoy her can still cancel later. Step 5 only showed that the first ברייתא did not disprove him. This ברייתא says clearly that silence meant to annoy does confirm the נדר. When a ברייתא directly contradicts an אמורא, the אמורא's view falls, and the גמרא signals this with the word תיובתא.

keyTerms.meaning: a full refutation; the view being challenged cannot stand

phrases.english: This is a refutation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the verdict on רב כהנא's challenge now that the ברייתא is complete.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The view that silence meant to annoy does not confirm the נדר is refuted by the ברייתא.

steps.title: Why not read one phrase as silence to confirm and the other as plain silence?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's reading. Perhaps the second phrase is only about silence with no particular intention, as step 5 suggested, and not about silence meant to annoy.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him explain it this way: this phrase is about one who is silent in order to confirm, and that phrase is about one who is silent with no particular intention!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the ברייתא. It asks why the extra phrase could not simply be about plain silence.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא assumed the second phrase must mean silence to annoy. But there is a third option: plain silence with no intention. If the phrase means that, the earlier view (silence to annoy does not confirm) could survive.

keyTerms.meaning: but let him explain it as
staying silent with no particular intention

phrases.english: But let him explain it this way:
this phrase is about one who is silent in order to confirm,
and that phrase is about one who is silent with no particular intention!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלוֹקֵים: הָא — בְּשׁוֹתֵק עַל מְנָת לְקַיֵּים, הָא — בְּשׁוֹתֵק סְתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the ברייתא's reading from step 10 by offering the reading used in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that the second phrase must be about silence to annoy.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another reading is possible (plain silence), so the ברייתא's conclusion is not forced.

steps.title: There are extra פסוקים about silence
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the תורה writes about silence more times than needed. The extra mentions teach that any kind of silence confirms, even silence meant to annoy.
steps.simpleTranslation: Extra verses are written.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the ברייתא's reading by pointing to the extra פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If there were only two mentions of silence, one could be for silence to confirm and one for plain silence. But the תורה mentions silence even more times. The extra mentions have to add something, so they include silence meant to annoy.
steps.whatToRemember: In the end, the ברייתא stands: because of the extra פסוקים, even silence meant to annoy confirms the נדר.

phrases.english: Extra verses are written.
phrases.notes: He means the תורה talks about the husband's silence more times than these two cases need.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The second phrase might only cover plain silence.
steps.terutzMaskana: The extra פסוקים include every kind of silence, even silence meant to annoy.

steps.title: רבא's challenge from a נדר made close to nightfall
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes a משנה: if a woman made a נדר just before nightfall, the husband can cancel only until dark. רבא asks why his silence should count against him. His silence was not meant to confirm, so it should be treated like silence meant to annoy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא challenged: If she made a נדר close to nightfall, he can cancel it for her until it gets dark. If he did not cancel and it got dark, he cannot cancel anymore. Why? Let it be like one who is silent in order to annoy!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings a second challenge against the view that silence meant to annoy does not confirm the נדר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי חנינא, a husband who stays silent to annoy her can still cancel even after the day has ended. This husband's silence before dark was not meant to confirm either, so he too should be able to cancel after nightfall. The משנה says he cannot, which goes against רבי חנינא.

phrases.english: Rava challenged:
If she made a vow close to nightfall,
he can cancel it for her until it gets dark,
because if he did not cancel and it got dark,
he can no longer cancel.
Why?
Let it be like one who is silent in order to annoy!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a new source against the same view that was refuted in step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that silence not meant to confirm, like silence to annoy, does not count as הקם.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה treats silence that was not meant to confirm as ending the right to cancel, which goes against that view.

steps.title: רבא's challenge is also a refutation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא declares רבא's challenge a full refutation as well.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rules that רבא's משנה also knocks down the earlier view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No answer is offered for רבא's question. So the view that silence meant to annoy does not confirm the נדר is refuted a second time.

phrases.english: This is a refutation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the verdict on רבא's challenge.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The earlier view is refuted again, this time by the משנה about nightfall.

steps.title: רב אשי begins a challenge from a husband who did not know the law
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי quotes a משנה. A husband who did not know that cancelling exists may still cancel later. A husband who did not know that this was a נדר is the subject of a מחלוקת between רבי מאיר and the חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי challenged: If he says 'I know there are vows, but I did not know there are people who cancel them,' he may cancel. If he says 'I know there are people who cancel, but I did not know this was a vow,' רבי מאיר says he may not cancel, and the חכמים say he may cancel.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי is setting up a third challenge by quoting a משנה. The actual argument against the earlier view comes in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This משנה is about a husband who stayed silent past the day because he did not know something. In the first case he may still cancel. In the second case רבי מאיר and the חכמים argue. רב אשי will use these cases to say something about silence that was not meant to confirm.

keyTerms.meaning: those who cancel; the fact that a נדר can be cancelled
the Sages, who say he may cancel

steps.confusionAlert: This step only quotes the משנה. רב אשי's actual point against the earlier view comes in the next step (step 17).

phrases.english: Rav Ashi challenged:
"I know that there are vows,
phrases.notes: This is the husband speaking after the day he heard the נדר has already passed.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁיֵּשׁ מְפִירִין״ — יָפֵר.
phrases.english: but I did not know that there are those who cancel" — he may cancel.
"I know that there are those who cancel,
but I did not know that this is a vow" —
Rabbi Meir says: he may not cancel,
and the Sages say: he may cancel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a third challenge after רבא's refutation.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that silence not meant to confirm does not count as הקם.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Set up only so far: the משנה's cases of silence caused by not knowing will be used against that view.

steps.title: Why not treat the unaware husband like one silent to annoy?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי finishes his challenge. According to רבי מאיר, the husband who did not know it was a נדר cannot cancel later. But his silence was not meant to confirm, so it should count like silence meant to annoy, and that kind of silence supposedly lets him cancel later.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why can he not cancel? Let him be treated like someone who kept quiet in order to annoy her!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי now asks his punch-line question about the משנה he quoted in step 16. If silence meant to annoy does not lock in a vow, why should this husband's silence lock it in?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband who did not know it was a נדר clearly never meant to confirm it. According to רבי חנינא, silence meant to annoy also does not confirm, and the husband can still cancel later. If so, רבי מאיר should let this husband cancel later too. Since רבי מאיר does not, the משנה seems to show that silence counts even without intent to confirm.

keyTerms.meaning: In order to annoy or provoke (her)

phrases.english: And why?
phrases.notes: He means: why can't this husband cancel later, according to רבי מאיר in the משנה from step 16?

phrases.english: Let him be like one who is silent in order to annoy!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַמַּאי? לֶיהֱוֵי כְּשׁוֹתֵק עַל מְנָת לְמֵיקַט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רב אשי's challenge by drawing the conclusion from the משנה quoted in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that silence meant to annoy does not confirm the vow and lets the husband cancel later.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under רבי מאיר, a husband who did not know it was a נדר cannot cancel later, even though his silence was not meant to confirm. So silence without intent to confirm still counts, which goes against the view being challenged.

steps.title: רב אשי's challenge is a full refutation
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that רב אשי's challenge cannot be answered. It is a full refutation of the view that silence meant to annoy lets the husband cancel later.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is a refutation.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא declares that רב אשי's question has no answer. The view that silence meant to annoy lets him cancel later is knocked down once again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same ending as in step 15 after רבא's challenge. Each attack, from the ברייתא, from רבא, and now from רב אשי, ends in a full refutation. The final result is that silence confirms a vow even when it was not meant to confirm.

keyTerms.meaning: A full refutation, meaning the view has been disproven

steps.whatToRemember: Every challenge ends in תיובתא. The final rule is that a husband's silence for a full day confirms the vow, even if he was silent only to annoy her.

phrases.english: A refutation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the challenge raised in steps 16 and 17.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The view that silence meant to annoy lets the husband cancel later is refuted. Silence confirms the vow even without intent to confirm.

steps.title: הדרן — Closing פרק נערה המאורסה
steps.stepSummary: The traditional closing line marks the end of the פרק called נערה המאורסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, נערה המאורסה.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the standard farewell line that ends a פרק. It is not part of the argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each פרק is named after its opening words. This פרק opened with the betrothed young woman, נערה המאורסה. The הדרן line closes it so that a new פרק can begin.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you (a closing formula for a פרק)
The betrothed young woman (the name of the פרק)

phrases.english: We will return to you, "The Betrothed Young Woman"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Formally closes the פרק after the final refutation.

steps.title: New פרק: vows of self-affliction can be cancelled
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה begins to list which vows a husband can cancel. The first category is vows that involve עינוי נפש, such as vows tied to bathing or not bathing, or to adorning or not adorning oneself.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the vows that he can cancel: matters that involve self-affliction. For example, "If I bathe" or "If I do not bathe," "If I adorn myself" or "If I do not adorn myself."
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק opens. The משנה starts listing the kinds of vows a husband (or father) is allowed to cancel, beginning with vows that cause her self-affliction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the topic was who can cancel and when. Now the question is which vows can be cancelled at all. The first category is עינוי נפש, vows that take away comfort or care of her body, like bathing and adorning. The examples come in pairs, "if I do" and "if I do not," which shows that the vow's wording can go either way.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole new פרק. A husband cannot cancel every vow, only certain categories, and עינוי נפש is the first.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not assume a husband can cancel any vow at all. This משנה is starting a list of specific categories he can cancel.

phrases.english: And these are the vows that he can cancel:
Matters that involve self-affliction:
"If I bathe" or "If I do not bathe,"
phrases.notes: This is a short way of quoting a vow tied to bathing. The משנה doesn't spell out the rest of the vow here.

phrases.english: "If I adorn myself" or "If I do not adorn myself."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new פרק after the הדרן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A husband can cancel vows that involve עינוי נפש, such as vows about bathing or adorning oneself.
